d9336104-5f87-448d-8072-1ff4ea7ba8df.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another
COURT: Supreme Court of India
CITATION: (2014) 8 SCC 273 : AIR 2014 SC 2756 : 2014 Cri LJ 3707
BENCH: Chandramauli Kr. Prasad and Pinaki Chandra Ghose, JJ.
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 2014-07-02
DOCUMENT TYPE: judgment

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

5611c338-0538-48bf-ad6c-83fbebbf4f4b.document:
[Para 3]
The petitioner in this special leave petition seeks anticipatory bail in a case registered under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The petitioner apprehends arrest following marital discord with his wife, who alleged demands for dowry.

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

6b71b5bb-414d-44fd-9812-4f2fc9875239.document:
[Para 5]
Arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom, and casts scars forever. Lawmakers know that arrest is a tool of harassment and oppression in hands of unscrupulous police officers. No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so. The existence of the power to arrest is one thing, the justification for the exercise of it is quite another. A police officer must not make arrests in a routine manner upon mere allegation of commission of an offence.

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

76e6ae16-a04c-4ae7-8ab3-b26c718c1231.document: [Para 7] Section 41 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 provides the conditions under which police may arrest without warrant. In respect of offences punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years, arrest must not be made routinely. The police officer must be satisfied that such arrest is necessary: (a) to prevent such person from committing any further offence; or (b) for proper investigation of the offence; or (c) to prevent such person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear or tampering with such evidence; or

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

ded13332-78b8-45df-a568-e5db9dff6262.document: person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear or tampering with such evidence; or (d) to prevent such person from making any inducement, threat, or promise to witnesses; or (e) to ensure his presence before the court whenever required.

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

4efe63f3-3f3c-4e64-8e6c-aff8a7c18e1f.document:
[Para 8]
Section 41A of the Code provides that where the arrest of a person is not required under Section 41(1), the police officer shall issue a notice directing the person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made to appear before him. Where such a notice is issued, it shall be the duty of that person to comply with the terms of the notice. So long as he complies with the notice, he shall not be arrested unless the police officer records reasons in writing.

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

2cbe73dd-4a6c-4609-8cd7-c7b40c26438d.document: [Para 11] To ensure that police officers do not arrest accused persons unnecessarily and Magistrates do not authorise detention casually, this court issues the following mandatory directions: 1. All State Governments shall instruct police officers not to automatically arrest when a case under Section 498A IPC or offences with punishment up to 7 years is registered. 2. Police officers shall be provided with a checklist containing specified sub-clauses under Section 41(1)(b)(ii). 3. The police officer shall forward the checklist duly filled and furnish reasons necessitating arrest when producing

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

5b3498dd-d756-4d4e-bfa4-b7ff984fe2f5.document: shall forward the checklist duly filled and furnish reasons necessitating arrest when producing the accused before the Magistrate. 4. The Magistrate shall peruse the report and record independent satisfaction before authorising further detention. 5. Notice of appearance in terms of Section 41A CrPC shall be served on the accused within two weeks from the date of institution of the case. 6. Failure to comply with these directions shall render the police officer and Magistrate liable for departmental action and contempt of court.

metadata.document_title: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Another

36ceb1d9-daab-462c-8628-8cf611bc0a49.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
COURT: Parliament of India / Statutory Enactment
CITATION: Act No. 46 of 2023, Section 482
BENCH: Statutory Provision
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 2023-12-25
DOCUMENT TYPE: statute

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

f2b37371-5046-49b4-afca-06bea0550a47.document: [Section 482(1)] Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest: Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail; and that Court may, after taking into consideration, inter alia, the following factors, namely: (i) the nature and gravity of the accusation; (ii) the antecedents of the applicant including the fact as to whether he has previously undergone imprisonment

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

7e3f4ce1-d865-4733-aecc-053d91a7ec9d.document: of the applicant including the fact as to whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on conviction in respect of any cognizable offence; (iii) the possibility of the applicant to flee from justice; and (iv) where the accusation has been made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant by having him so arrested, either reject the application forthwith or issue an interim order for the grant of bail.

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

41812406-115d-4f01-833d-0b44026bbf05.document: [Section 482(2)] When the High Court or Court of Session makes a direction under sub-section (1), it may include such conditions in such directions in the light of the facts of the particular case, as it may think fit, including: (i) a condition that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required; (ii) a condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer; (iii)

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

5e8827c6-e109-49df-9596-ead35f73d6a8.document: case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer; (iii) a condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court; (iv) such other condition as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of section 480, as if the bail were granted under that section.

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

cd9f312f-d7ee-443b-87b9-d1edb08365f9.document:
[Section 482(3)]
The presence of the applicant seeking anticipatory bail shall not be mandatory at the time of hearing of the application, unless the Court considers it necessary in the interest of justice.

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

6e897899-41e7-4914-9c7e-b853a075ccc4.document:
[Section 482(4)]
Nothing in this section shall apply to any case involving the arrest of any person on accusation of having committed an offence under section 65 or section 66 or sub-section (2) of section 70 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

metadata.document_title: Section 482, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

67c7c4dc-80da-4eb5-8117-970a9146bde6.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Article 21, Constitution of India
COURT: Constituent Assembly of India / Constitutional Law
CITATION: Constitution of India, Part III, Article 21
BENCH: Constitutional Guarantee
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 1950-01-26
DOCUMENT TYPE: statute

metadata.document_title: Article 21, Constitution of India

2f6a5e1c-f7e1-462f-bc71-6a0e84901e36.document:
[Article 21]
Protection of life and personal liberty:
No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.

metadata.document_title: Article 21, Constitution of India

b57bdd05-b99e-4698-81f6-f35542f0f678.document:
[Constitutional Jurisprudence]
In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) 1 SCC 248, the Supreme Court ruled that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be right, just, and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. A procedure that deprives an individual of their personal liberty through unjust or mechanical arrest violates the core guarantee of Article 21.

metadata.document_title: Article 21, Constitution of India

ef2f8252-0648-4ee1-8b43-e784fec0b7ce.document: Anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is intrinsically linked to Article 21. As observed in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and affirmed in Sushila Aggarwal, the judicial discretion to grant pre-arrest bail protects innocent citizens from the irreparable trauma, stigmatization, and indignity of unwarranted incarceration pending trial.

metadata.document_title: Article 21, Constitution of India

DOCUMENT TITLE: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)
COURT: Supreme Court of India / Parliament of India
CITATION: Central Act No. 2 of 1974, Section 154 and (2014) 2 SCC 1 (Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.)
BENCH: 5-Judge Constitution Bench (P. Sathasivam, C.J., B.S. Chauhan, Ranjana P. Desai, Ranjan Gogoi, S.A. Bobde, JJ.)
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 2013-11-12
DOCUMENT TYPE: statute

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

0f8d19f1-79b5-45c0-a3d9-4afeab92ab48.document: [Section 154(1): Mandatory Registration of First Information Report (FIR)] Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence (such as theft of a ring, robbery, assault, cheating, or burglary), if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

a86447a2-960f-4a19-96c0-caf7115212a7.document: substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may prescribe in this behalf. A copy of the information as recorded under sub-section (1) shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant.

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

9fe558a5-8427-41c1-9d34-efc42f037902.document: [Lalita Kumari Landmark Directives on FIR Registration] In Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1, the 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court held: 1. Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. 2. If the information received does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity for an inquiry, a preliminary inquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not. 3. Cases involving theft

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

776c33ff-8aa3-4ece-80dd-c7709a4aea6a.document: only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not. 3. Cases involving theft of personal property, stolen rings, gold, vehicles, or physical robbery unequivocally disclose a cognizable offence; police officers cannot refuse to register an FIR on the grounds of lack of jurisdiction or delay. 4. Concept of Zero FIR: A victim or informant can approach any police station to lodge an FIR (Zero FIR) irrespective of where the theft occurred. The police station must record the FIR, assign a serial number zero, and immediately transfer the case to the jurisdictional police station for investigation.

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

15e16ef9-6dfb-452d-a9f5-bc2b58919e90.document: zero, and immediately transfer the case to the jurisdictional police station for investigation.

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

54981597-248c-4b21-8d50-aac9cbc8340d.document:
[Section 154(3): Remedy when Police Refuse to Register FIR]
Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record the information referred to in sub-section (1) may send the substance of such information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by any police officer subordinate to him.

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

f198b86f-c829-4961-b53f-a2bb7adb71d1.document:
[Section 173, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS Reform on FIR & e-FIR)]
Section 173 of BNSS 2023 replaces Section 154 CrPC, formalizing electronic FIRs (e-FIRs) and Zero FIR:
Sub-section (1) permits every information relating to a cognizable offence to be given orally or by electronic communication (e-FIR), irrespective of the area where the crime was committed. Where information is given electronically, it shall be taken on record upon being signed within three days by the person giving it.

metadata.document_title: Section 154, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (FIR Registration & Lalita Kumari Ruling)

235d5490-1c75-4ec4-a0c7-5d4cb003cf13.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Section 156(3), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Magistrate's Power to Order Investigation)
COURT: Parliament of India / Supreme Court Precedents
CITATION: Central Act No. 2 of 1974, Section 156(3) and (2008) 2 SCC 409 (Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P.)
BENCH: Statutory Procedure & Supreme Court Precedents
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 1974-01-25
DOCUMENT TYPE: statute

metadata.document_title: Section 156(3), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Magistrate's Power to Order Investigation)

2657793d-ae73-4e56-8739-6bcbc3a0a235.document:
[Section 156(1) and (2): Police Officer's Power to Investigate Cognizable Offence]
Any officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try under the provisions of Chapter XIII.
No proceeding of a police officer in any such case shall at any stage be called in question on the ground that the case was one which such officer was not empowered under this section to investigate.

metadata.document_title: Section 156(3), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Magistrate's Power to Order Investigation)

8cd15f3b-036a-4d75-86a6-ba6ae8b53123.document: [Section 156(3): Judicial Magistrate's Power to Order FIR and Investigation] Any Magistrate empowered under section 190 may order such an investigation as above-mentioned. Remedy when Police Station Refuses FIR: If a citizen's complaint regarding theft, stolen property, fraud, or cheating is rejected or ignored by the local police station and the Superintendent of Police under Section 154(3) fails to act, the aggrieved person can file an application under Section 156(3) CrPC before the jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate. Landmark Ruling: In Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P. (2008) 2 SCC 409, the Supreme

metadata.document_title: Section 156(3), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Magistrate's Power to Order Investigation)

c7e527a3-21b6-425f-9115-2f657ff73b61.document: Judicial Magistrate. Landmark Ruling: In Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P. (2008) 2 SCC 409, the Supreme Court held that Section 156(3) CrPC provides a comprehensive, effective alternative remedy. The Magistrate has wide powers to ensure proper investigation, including ordering the registration of an FIR and monitoring the progress of the investigation.

metadata.document_title: Section 156(3), Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Magistrate's Power to Order Investigation)

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

27790ff1-019a-493d-96a7-2f72fe73a1bc.document: [Section 438(1)] Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest: Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail; and that Court may, after taking into consideration, inter alia, the following factors, namely: (i) the nature and gravity of the accusation; (ii) the antecedents of the applicant including the fact as to whether he has previously undergone imprisonment

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

b8ff5cf5-bfa1-4d42-84e2-3068d55944b6.document: of the applicant including the fact as to whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on conviction in respect of any cognizable offence; (iii) the possibility of the applicant to flee from justice; and (iv) where the accusation has been made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant by having him so arrested, either reject the application forthwith or issue an interim order for the grant of anticipatory bail.

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

8222b06a-a126-43c6-a367-076d466bbd0c.document: [Section 438(2)] When the High Court or the Court of Session makes a direction under sub-section (1), it may include such conditions in such directions in the light of the facts of the particular case, as it may think fit, including: (i) a condition that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required; (ii) a condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer;

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

b50fa617-74a1-48ca-8d85-91180f157061.document: of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer; (iii) a condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court; (iv) such other condition as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of section 437, as if the bail were granted under that section.

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

c00dd676-2d38-4428-b246-9f4356ee367a.document:
[Section 438(3)]
If such person is thereafter arrested without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station on such accusation, and is prepared either at the time of arrest or at any time while in the custody of such officer to give bail, he shall be released on bail; and if a Magistrate taking cognizance of such offence decides that a warrant should issue in the first instance against that person, he shall issue a bailable warrant in conformity with the direction of the Court under sub-section (1).

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

d95301fb-0d8f-442c-a4e0-99f5f1bc5b10.document:
[Section 438(4)]
Nothing in this section shall apply to any case involving the arrest of any person on accusation of having committed an offence under sub-section (3) of section 376 or section 376AB or section 376DA or section 376DB of the Indian Penal Code.

metadata.document_title: Section 438, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

38bfac88-c62a-45ec-87c6-e95fa262aaa7.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab
COURT: Supreme Court of India (Constitution Bench)
CITATION: (1980) 2 SCC 565 : AIR 1980 SC 1632 : 1980 Cri LJ 1125
BENCH: Y.V. Chandrachud, C.J., P.N. Bhagwati, N.L. Untwalia, V.D. Tulzapurkar, and A.P. Sen, JJ.
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 1980-04-09
DOCUMENT TYPE: judgment

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

b9567e99-a247-44f4-8630-3da02e8655a1.document:
[Para 1]
This appeal by special leave involves the interpretation of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which confers power on the High Court and the Court of Session to grant anticipatory bail. The question before this Constitution Bench is regarding the scope, nature, and limitations governing the exercise of judicial discretion under Section 438 of the Code.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

2fc91b1d-df39-43e4-9a70-b684d739f883.document:
[Para 7]
Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 makes a departure from the previous Code of 1898 by introducing a provision for the grant of anticipatory bail. The Law Commission of India in its 41st Report recommended the introduction of this provision in order to safeguard the personal liberty of citizens against malicious, frivolous, or politically motivated accusations intended to humiliate, disgrace, or incarcerate individuals before trial.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

f0bc3cf0-d781-48d1-b06c-cfa574bfe733.document:
[Para 12]
The power under Section 438 is of an extraordinary character and must be exercised with due care and circumspection. However, the discretion vested in the High Court and the Court of Session is not bound by rigid or inflexible fetters. The Legislature intentionally refrained from circumscribing the discretion with rigid rules. The High Court and the Court of Session must be left free to exercise their judicial discretion according to the facts and circumstances of each individual case.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

b52f30d5-7cf8-429a-97a2-5ffd2b554d9e.document: [Para 15] While considering an application for anticipatory bail under Section 438, the court must carefully evaluate several critical factors: First, the nature and gravity of the accusation and the exact role attributed to the applicant. Second, the antecedents of the applicant, including whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on conviction in respect of any cognizable offence. Third, the possibility of the applicant fleeing from justice or absconding. Fourth, whether the accusation has been made with the ulterior motive of injuring, humiliating, or tarnishing the reputation of the

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

e4e711e3-5bd9-4272-acc7-14cac2237b06.document: been made with the ulterior motive of injuring, humiliating, or tarnishing the reputation of the applicant by having him so arrested. Fifth, the likelihood of the accused tampering with evidence, threatening witnesses, or otherwise obstructing the course of fair investigation and trial.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

83d71036-7542-4264-9a08-ed349dff526c.document:
[Para 19]
A blanket order of anticipatory bail cannot and ought not to be granted. A blanket order that an applicant shall be released on bail whenever he may be arrested in future for any offence whatsoever serves as a charter of lawlessness and impedes the legitimate functions of the investigating agency. An applicant seeking anticipatory bail must demonstrate a reasonable belief and apprehension of arrest founded on specific and tangible facts relating to a concrete offence.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

6a8898c7-139a-4592-a15e-fe4091bd95a9.document: [Para 26] The court granting anticipatory bail is empowered under Section 438(2) to impose suitable conditions. Such conditions include: (i) A condition that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required; (ii) A condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat, or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the court or to any police officer; (iii) A condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

245489d5-2e75-4cdb-9e9c-22220bd4cfce.document: (iii) A condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the court; and (iv) Such other condition as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of Section 437, as if the bail were granted under that section.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

783ba0f7-a750-404c-aa8c-b7c538ffb9cc.document:
[Para 31]
Anticipatory bail does not place the accused beyond the reach of the investigating machinery. If custodial interrogation becomes indispensable on discovery of new material during the course of investigation, the prosecution is always at liberty to apply to the court for cancellation or modification of the anticipatory bail order under Section 439(2) of the Code.

metadata.document_title: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others v. State of Punjab

1a9b1239-52d7-4a09-bb03-2ebd1f9192c4.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)
COURT: Parliament of India / Statutory Criminal Enactment
CITATION: Central Act No. 45 of 1860, Sections 378, 379 (Corresponding to Section 303, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023)
BENCH: Statutory Criminal Code
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 1860-10-06
DOCUMENT TYPE: statute

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

0b3b98d0-4a76-4114-8b9b-456eabcf77e0.document: [Section 378: Definition and Ingredients of Theft] Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. Explanation 1: A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth. Explanation 2: A moving effected by the same act which affects the severance may be a theft. Explanation 3: A person is said to cause a thing

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

c8ebbf4a-97b2-49bb-b5cf-53c45ea81b7f.document: act which affects the severance may be a theft. Explanation 3: A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it. Explanation 4: A person who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal. Explanation 5: The consent mentioned in the definition may be express or implied, and may be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

65da5637-af99-4a9c-9dc4-c9a550f1d4d8.document: and may be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied. Illustrations: (a) A cuts down a tree on Z's ground, with the intention of dishonestly taking the tree out of Z's possession without Z's consent. Here, as soon as A has severed the tree in order to such taking, he has committed theft. (b) A puts a bait for dogs in his pocket, and thus induces Z's dog to follow it. Here, if A's intention be dishonestly to take the dog out of Z's possession without Z's consent, A has committed theft as soon as Z's dog has begun to follow

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

06e4d5f6-8e79-4649-b529-30d720ebcbe0.document: of Z's possession without Z's consent, A has committed theft as soon as Z's dog has begun to follow A. (c) A meets a bullock carrying a box of treasure. He drives the bullock in a certain direction, in order that he may dishonestly take the treasure. As soon as the bullock begins to move, A has committed theft of the treasure. (d) If any person takes an article of jewellery, gold ring, diamond ring, watch, purse, money, mobile phone, or any valuable movable property belonging to another person without consent and with dishonest intention, such act constitutes the offence of theft.

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

0ef571c2-f1a0-40c9-8a0f-88836a071813.document:
[Section 379: Punishment for Theft]
Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
Legal Classification: The offence of theft under Section 379 IPC is a cognizable offence, meaning the police have the authority and statutory duty to register an FIR and arrest the accused without a warrant. It is triable by any Magistrate and is a non-bailable offence.

metadata.document_title: Section 378 and 379, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Theft)

84c02718-6347-4802-8b37-9fd94e3cad5f.document: [Section 303, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS Reform)] Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 replaces Sections 378 and 379 of the Indian Penal Code. Sub-section (1) defines theft with identical essential ingredients (dishonest taking of movable property out of possession without consent). Sub-section (2) provides that whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. In cases of community service for petty theft where the value of stolen property is less than five thousand rupees

3707af90-0cea-4f24-b810-a236ed386e60.document:
[Section 415: Definition of Cheating]
Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to cheat.

metadata.document_title: Section 415 and 420, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Cheating and Fraud)

52ccad1c-5a65-4e45-8b98-42f80a796523.document: [Section 420: Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property] Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Legal Classification: The offence under Section 420 IPC is cognizable, non-bailable, and triable by a Magistrate

metadata.document_title: Section 415 and 420, Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Cheating and Fraud)

cc099548-2a12-4af3-9786-3b1e31cc3e6b.document: The offence under Section 420 IPC is cognizable, non-bailable, and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. An FIR under Section 154 CrPC can be lodged at the police station having territorial jurisdiction over the transaction or where the deceit took place.

[Section 318, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS Cheating)]
Section 318 of BNS 2023 replaces Sections 415 and 420 IPC. Sub-section (4) provides that whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces delivery of any property or valuable security shall be punished with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

DOCUMENT TITLE: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another
COURT: Supreme Court of India
CITATION: (2022) 10 SCC 51 : 2022 SCC OnLine SC 825 : AIR 2022 SC 3386
BENCH: Sanjay Kishan Kaul and M.M. Sundresh, JJ.
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 2022-07-11
DOCUMENT TYPE: judgment

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

7703f4c2-1596-4615-86bb-0ebd1f1b682e.document:
[Para 2]
The present proceedings arise out of persistent concerns regarding overcrowding of prisons in India, where over two-thirds of the inmate population comprises undertrial prisoners. This judgment issues comprehensive guidelines to streamline the procedure for grant of bail, emphasizing that the rule is bail and not jail.

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

a4d84050-57d7-4e6f-b965-5fa709450322.document: [Para 18] Offences are broadly categorized into four groups for the purpose of bail consideration: Category A: Offences punishable with imprisonment of 7 years or less not falling under Category B and D. For these offences, ordinary summons or appearance notice under Section 41A CrPC should be issued, and routine arrests avoided. Category B: Offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for more than 7 years. Bail applications to be decided on merits on appearance. Category C: Offences punishable under special Acts containing stringent negative bail conditions (such as

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

a86d045f-eb70-4a02-a893-3f8bbb14e186.document: C: Offences punishable under special Acts containing stringent negative bail conditions (such as NDPS Act S. 37, PMLA S. 45, UAPA S. 43D(5), Companies Act S. 212(6)). Category D: Economic offences not covered by special Acts. The gravity of financial loss to the public exchequer and systemic ramification must be considered.

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

f21b13a7-71a7-4d83-9242-fdf444f72fb7.document:
[Para 26]
While dealing with applications under Section 438 of the CrPC, courts must balance the need for custodial interrogation against the fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21. Economic offences do not fall under a single blanket rule; where the accused has cooperated with the investigation, furnished requisite documentary records, and has deep roots in society without flight risk, anticipatory bail should not be refused merely on the ground of an economic accusation.

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

c78f902a-8372-4a27-bf34-5e894f4c7648.document:
[Para 33]
Courts must not impose mechanical or excessively harsh conditions while granting bail. Requiring local sureties or exorbitant monetary bonds that an impoverished undertrial cannot furnish defeats the very purpose of bail and violates Article 21 of the Constitution.

metadata.document_title: Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Another

1921b5d9-82a4-402a-952f-47295f476268.document:
DOCUMENT TITLE: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another
COURT: Supreme Court of India (Constitution Bench)
CITATION: (2020) 5 SCC 1 : 2020 SCC OnLine SC 98 : AIR 2020 SC 831
BENCH: Arun Mishra, Indira Banerjee, Vineet Saran, M.R. Shah, and S. Ravindra Bhat, JJ.
DATE OF JUDGMENT: 2020-01-29
DOCUMENT TYPE: judgment

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

b6217479-76ad-45f9-8c49-ad452e154669.document:
[Para 5]
The primary questions referred to this Constitution Bench are:
(1) Whether the protection granted to a person under Section 438 CrPC should be limited to a fixed period so as to enable the person to surrender before the trial court and seek regular bail; and
(2) Whether the life of an anticipatory bail order should end automatically upon the filing of the charge sheet under Section 173(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure or upon the summoning of the accused by the trial court.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

e88c29b0-15a4-4f98-ad93-0045679d4909.document:
[Para 63]
On question No. 1, this court holds that the protection granted under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 should not ordinarily be limited to a fixed period. The life of an anticipatory bail order does not automatically end when the charge sheet or final report is filed by the police under Section 173 CrPC. The order of anticipatory bail can continue till the conclusion of the trial, unless there are exceptional or special circumstances requiring the court to limit its duration.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

4d81f9b0-9651-47d8-bbf8-f13964b8b329.document:
[Para 74]
Judicial discretion should be exercised flexibly. When the High Court or Sessions Court considers an application for anticipatory bail, it is open to the court to impose conditions or restrict the duration if the specific facts of the case demand such limitation. However, limiting the order of anticipatory bail invariably in all cases is contrary to the legislative intent of Section 438 CrPC and the ratio laid down in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

469466c3-38b0-4706-bf32-d14bf5cccb49.document:
[Para 78]
On question No. 2, the Constitution Bench clarifies that the mere filing of a charge sheet under Section 173(2) CrPC or the taking of cognizance by the magistrate does not ipso facto terminate or extinguish an order of anticipatory bail. The accused is not obligated to surrender and apply afresh for regular bail merely because the charge sheet has been submitted to the court.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

0d7ae82c-6938-4e26-bf0e-86bde55db2b2.document:
[Para 82]
It is also reiterated that anticipatory bail granted to an accused can always be cancelled or recalled by the High Court or Sessions Court under Section 439(2) CrPC if the accused breaches any bail condition, tampers with witness testimonies, intimidates victims, absconds, or misuses his liberty in any manner that prejudices a fair trial.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another

444efbf1-487a-4317-9572-d7b723fc7e39.document:
[Para 91]
In conclusion, personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution is a paramount value. Section 438 CrPC embodies this constitutional value by providing a procedural shield against unjustified arrests, while balancing the imperative requirements of state investigation and public interest.

metadata.document_title: Sushila Aggarwal and Others v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Another
